findings.where: The full-width blue 'Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform' band with its Subscribe button, right below the hero (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: A second call to action, set in large white display type on a full field of house blue, is louder than the one real action, the 'Write to me directly' email box. In the overview it is the most saturated thing on the page and catches the eye before the address does. The brief asks for one message and one quiet contact.
findings.who_objects: The bank official, who has just decided to write to Mark and is pulled toward a newsletter sign-up instead. The founder also objects: his brief sets one direct, personal way to reach Mark, and the band breaks it.

findings.where: The Subscribe button in the blue briefings band (parts p6, a link to #subscribe)
findings.fault: The button goes to #subscribe, and the page has no subscribe section or form. Clicking the page's loudest button does nothing a visitor can see.
findings.who_objects: Any visitor who clicks Subscribe, finds nothing happens, and starts to doubt the site works at all. That is a bad first impression for an advisor to governments.

findings.where: The briefings band's heading, 'Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform'
findings.fault: The heading switches to a marketer's third person ('Mark's') right after a hero in Mark's first-person voice. It also promises a 'briefings' product that no source says exists. It reads as a salesy newsletter push, not a personal advisor speaking.
findings.who_objects: The founder: his brief requires first person, never invented claims, and nothing salesy. The senior official also notices the change of voice and distrusts it.

findings.where: The article specimen: the body paragraphs, the paragraph under the 'chapter topics' subhead, and the three-item numbered list (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The long-form body text is centred, so every line starts at a different place. In the list, the second lines of each item centre under the first, and the blue numbers float away from their text. Centred blocks of several lines are slow and tiring to read, and the list barely scans as a list.
findings.who_objects: The official reading Mark's article to judge his thinking on PPP law, who has to hunt for the start of each line through a long piece. The brief calls the article page the product.

findings.where: The PDF lecture card, 'Streamlining the PPP Process…', at the end of the article specimen
findings.fault: The card stacks a pale blue fill, a blue hairline border, rounded corners and a wide soft drop shadow, all on one resting element. It is the only rounded, shadowed card on an otherwise flat, square page, so it reads like a generic app or ad tile, not a publication in a legal journal.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who wants refined, never slick. A reader may also take the card for a promotion and skip it, though the PDF list is meant to be the product.

findings.where: Blue used on static text: the 'PALETTE' label (tracked blue capitals, parts p7) and the numbers of the article list
findings.fault: The page's own note says 'blue only where something can be clicked', and its type note says 'never tracked capitals', yet a static label and the list numbers are set in the link blue. The 'PALETTE' label is also in tracked capitals. Blue text that does nothing teaches the visitor that blue doesn't always mean a link.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who tries the blue list numbers or label and finds they do nothing. Angélique also loses a clear rule to copy when she adds content.

findings.where: Section labels below the fold: 'PALETTE' (blue tracked capitals), 'Type pair', 'An article page' and 'Motion sketch' (small bold sans), and 'Texture' (large italic serif)
findings.fault: Labels that do the same job get three different treatments, so the sections don't read as one consistent set.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who is judging whether the system holds together and what Angélique could repeat. The labels suggest it doesn't.

findings.where: The hero's nav bar: 'Mark M. Moseley' beside the MMM Infra mark
findings.fault: The nav holds only the name and the logo: no About, Work or Articles, and no Contact label. The name is static text (parts p1), while the logo beside it is a link. A visitor who wants Mark's track record has nowhere to go, and the white mark is larger and heavier than the name it should sit after.
findings.who_objects: The official, who wants his CV and past mandates before writing, and finds no route to them from the first screen. The founder also objects, since he asked that Mark's name lead.

findings.where: The hero's first screen: heading and lede
findings.fault: Nothing on the first screen says Mark is a lawyer or drafts PPP laws. The lede says only 'I advise … on infrastructure', and there is no evidence of work (named bodies, regions, a recent talk). A visitor looking for a legal advisor on a PPP law can't tell this is the right person, or why to trust him.
findings.who_objects: The bank official, who is choosing an individual against terms of reference. The founder also objects: the brief requires the page to reflect law, PPP and advice to governments.

findings.where: The MMM Infra mark and wordmark reversed to warm white in the hero nav
findings.fault: The hero uses a white version of the logo that the client doesn't hold. The house rule allows a version like this only with the client's yes, and nothing says that yes was given.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose logo has been recoloured without his say.

findings.where: The hero photograph's keyed edge, around Mark's head and shoulders against the slate ground
findings.fault: The grade keys the purple backdrop to slate, which leaves a visible cut-out rim around the hair and shoulder. Mark looks pasted onto the ground rather than photographed in it, the reverse of the brief's 'real people in real light'.
findings.who_objects: The founder, and any visitor who notices the cut-out look and reads the page as cheaply made.
